title: Cast Care & Neurovascular Assessment
summary: Monitoring and caring for a patient with a cast to detect early neurovascular compromise.
steps: Perform neurovascular assessment every 1–4 hours in the acute period. Use the '5 P's':
Pain: is it proportionate to the injury? Pain out of proportion = compartment syndrome.
Pallor: assess skin color distal to cast. Pale or cyanotic = vascular compromise.
Paresthesia: tingling or numbness = nerve compression.
Paralysis: inability to move fingers/toes = neurological or severe vascular compromise.
Pulse (Pulselessness): assess pulse distal to cast. Absent pulse = arterial compromise. Use Doppler if not palpable.
Compare to contralateral extremity for all assessments.
Monitor skin at cast edges: assess for redness, blistering, or skin breakdown.
Instruct patient: do NOT insert objects inside the cast. Report any foul odor, increased pain, or drainage.
Elevate extremity above heart level for first 24–48 hours to reduce edema.
Plaster cast: takes 24–48h to dry fully. Handle with palms (not fingers) to prevent indentations.
Fiberglass cast: dries in 30–60 minutes. More durable and water-resistant.
safetyTips: Pain out of proportion to injury + paresthesia + pallor = compartment syndrome. Notify provider immediately.
Do NOT bivalve, windowing, or loosen cast without provider order — may reduce fracture stability.
Foreign objects inside the cast cause pressure injuries and infections — strict education required.
documentation: Neurovascular status hourly in acute period
keyTakeaways: 5 P's: Pain, Pallor, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Pulselessness
Pain out of proportion = compartment syndrome

title: Compartment Syndrome Assessment
summary: Recognizing and reporting acute compartment syndrome, a limb-threatening emergency.
equipment: Compartment pressure monitor (if ordered by provider)
steps: KNOW THE RISK: compartment syndrome most common after tibial fracture, forearm fracture, crush injury, circumferential burns, and tight casts.
THE 5 P'S (in order of earliest to latest):
1. Pain: disproportionate to injury. Worsens with passive stretch of muscles in the compartment.
2. Paresthesia: tingling, numbness distal to compartment.
3. Pressure: tense, wooden feel of the extremity on palpation.
4. Pallor: pale or dusky distal skin (late sign).
5. Pulselessness: absence of distal pulse (very late — if present, ischemia is severe).
PASSIVE STRETCH TEST: gently dorsiflex the toes/fingers (stretches the muscles in the compartment). Severe pain = positive test = compartment syndrome until proven otherwise.
Remove all external wrappings: loosen/bivalve cast, remove splint padding, cut circumferential dressings.
Notify surgeon IMMEDIATELY. This is a surgical emergency.
Do NOT elevate above heart — reduces perfusion pressure to the compartment.
Fasciotomy is the definitive treatment. Damage is irreversible after 6–8 hours of ischemia.
safetyTips: Compartment syndrome can develop under a cast, after revascularization, or hours after injury.
Pulselessness is a LATE sign — do not wait for it. Act on pain + paresthesia.
Do NOT elevate the limb (reduces perfusion). Position at heart level.
keyTakeaways: Pain out of proportion = red flag
Passive stretch test is the earliest clinical sign

title: Crutch Walking & Gait Training
summary: Teaching and supervising proper axillary crutch use and gait patterns.
steps: FIT CRUTCHES: patient stands upright in crutches. 2–3 finger-widths between axilla and crutch pad (prevents axillary nerve compression). Elbows slightly flexed (20–30°). Handgrips at hip level.
Instruct: weight through hands on grips — NEVER rest axilla on the crutch pad.
NON-WEIGHT-BEARING (NWB): affected leg off the ground. 3-point gait: advance both crutches and affected leg forward together, then swing good leg through.
PARTIAL WEIGHT-BEARING (PWB): touch-down or percentage of weight on affected leg. 3-point gait: advance crutches + affected leg, then step good leg through.
WEIGHT-BEARING AS TOLERATED (WBAT): same 3-point or 4-point gait as tolerated.
SITTING DOWN: back up to chair edge. Transfer both crutches to one hand. Place other hand on armrest. Lower yourself to seat.
STANDING UP: both crutches in one hand on affected side. Push up with good leg and arm on armrest.
STAIRS — going UP: good leg first, then crutches + affected leg (good goes to heaven).
STAIRS — going DOWN: crutches + affected leg first, then good leg (bad goes down).
safetyTips: Axillary crutch palsy (radial nerve): from resting armpit on crutch pad. Emphasize weight on hands.
Confirm weight-bearing status with surgeon BEFORE ambulation teaching — NWB vs. WBAT are very different.
Monitor for fatigue in elderly patients — crutch walking is physically demanding.
keyTakeaways: Good goes to heaven (up stairs first)

title: Skin & Skeletal Traction Care
summary: Maintaining traction setup and monitoring for neurovascular compromise and skin integrity.
steps: Assess traction setup at every assessment: ropes are taut, pulleys are aligned, weights hang freely (not on bed or floor).
NEVER remove or lift weights without a provider order — disrupts fracture alignment.
Maintain correct alignment: body is in a straight line. Hip/knee at prescribed angles. Foot of bed elevated per order (countertraction).
NEUROVASCULAR ASSESSMENT q2–4h: 5 P's — pain, pallor, paresthesia, paralysis, pulselessness.
Skin care: inspect skin under traction boots or foam padding every shift for breakdown.
Skin traction: monitor for blistering, redness, or itching under the straps. Skin traction is for temporary use only.
Skeletal traction (pin/wire): pin site care per order (usually NS or H2O2 per policy). Assess for infection: redness, warmth, purulent drainage, loosening pin.
Trapeze bar: instruct patient to use it to lift themselves for back care and bedpan.
Log roll technique for position changes — maintain alignment.
Assess for complications: pressure injuries (heels, sacrum), DVT, atelectasis, constipation.
safetyTips: Weights are therapeutic — elevating or removing them disrupts fracture healing. Never remove without explicit order.
Pin site infection leads to osteomyelitis. Strict pin site care and aseptic technique are essential.
DVT is a major risk in traction patients — ensure pharmacologic prophylaxis is ordered.

title: External Fixator Pin Site Care
summary: Maintaining pin site cleanliness to prevent infection in patients with external fixation devices.
equipment: Sterile NS or chlorhexidine per protocol
steps: Perform pin site care per protocol frequency (daily to twice daily).
Perform hand hygiene. Don sterile gloves.
Assess each pin site: redness, warmth, swelling, drainage (serous is normal — purulent is not), skin tenting around pin.
Serous drainage that dries around the pin (crusting) = normal. Do NOT aggressively remove all crusting in the first weeks as it acts as a natural seal.
After the initial healing phase (typically 48–72 hours): clean crusts that are accumulating or causing skin tension using NS-moistened applicators with a gentle twisting motion.
Clean each pin site with a SEPARATE applicator — never use the same applicator on two pins.
Apply chlorhexidine or NS per order. Allow to air dry.
Apply loose gauze if ordered — tight dressings restrict drainage and promote infection.
Assess fixator frame for stability, loosening, or corrosion.
Instruct patient to avoid submerging pins in water.
safetyTips: Pin site infection leads to osteomyelitis — the most serious complication of external fixation.
Loosening of pins = pin tract infection suspected until proven otherwise. Notify orthopedic surgeon.
Skin tenting = skin being pulled by the pin as it loosens. Report to surgeon promptly.
